passages.t: ‘How can I curse what God has not cursed?’
passages.happening:
Balaam tells Balak to build seven altars and to prepare seven bulls and seven rams (verse 1). They offer a bull and a ram on each. Balaam goes off alone to a bare height. God meets him there and puts a message in his mouth (verses 3-5).

He returns and speaks his first oracle. Balak brought him from Aram to curse Jacob. “How can I curse what God has not cursed? How can I denounce what the LORD has not denounced?” (verse 8). He sees Israel from the cliffs: ‘a people dwelling apart, not reckoning themselves among the nations’ (verse 9). “Who can count the dust of Jacob or number even a fourth of Israel? Let me die the death of the righteous; let my end be like theirs!” (verse 10).

Balak protests that he hired Balaam to curse his enemies. Balaam answers, “Should I not speak exactly what the LORD puts in my mouth?” (verse 12).
passages.hearers:
The contest begins, and Balak does everything properly by the standards of his world. Seven altars with a bull and a ram on each was a costly and impressive rite. Sacrifices were commonly offered before an omen was sought, and seers looked for signs in the offered animals or in events in nature. Balaam's walk to a bare height fits that pattern. Balak assumes that a god can be moved by the right technique.

What comes back is called an oracle. The Hebrew word, mashal, can mean a proverb or a parable. In these chapters it means a solemn saying in poetry. The lines come in pairs, the second repeating or building on the first, and ‘Jacob’ and ‘Israel’ are two names for the one people.

The first oracle says three things about Israel.

It cannot be cursed by a man, because God has not cursed it. A seer's words have no power of their own.

It is a people apart. Israel's difference from the nations was not a matter of pride. God had set it apart for his own purpose.

It is beyond counting. ‘The dust of Jacob’ takes up God's promise to Abraham, that his offspring would be like the dust of the earth (Genesis 13:16). The seer from Aram, the land Abraham's family came from, looks down at the tents and sees the old promise kept.

Then comes a sigh. Balaam wishes that he might die the death of the righteous. It is the saddest line in the oracle, because the book later records how he did die: by the sword, among Israel's enemies (31:8). He saw what was good, and said so beautifully, and did not choose it.

The reader should remember where Israel is while this is said. The people are in the valley, unaware. And they are the same people who complained about the manna a few chapters ago. God says none of that to their enemy. He speaks of them only in terms of his promise.
passages.later:
God had said to Abraham, “I will make your offspring like the dust of the earth, so that if one could count the dust of the earth, then your offspring could be counted” (Genesis 13:16).

Paul puts Balaam's first question in his own way for the church: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Romans 8:31). And he asks, “Who will bring any charge against God’s elect? It is God who justifies” (Romans 8:33).
passages.asks: Balaam admired the end of the righteous and did not take their road. Ask what you admire in the lives of faithful people without wanting what it would cost you. And ask whether you believe that no word spoken against you can undo what God has spoken over you.

passages.t: ‘God is not a man, that He should lie’
passages.happening:
Balak tries a different place. He takes Balaam to the field of Zophim on the top of Pisgah, where only the edge of the camp can be seen, and builds seven more altars (verses 13-14). Again God meets Balaam and gives him words.

The second oracle is addressed to Balak by name. “God is not a man, that He should lie, or a son of man, that He should change His mind. Does He speak and not act? Does He promise and not fulfill?” (verse 19). “I have indeed received a command to bless; He has blessed, and I cannot change it” (verse 20).

“The LORD their God is with them, and the shout of the King is among them” (verse 21). God brought them out of Egypt. “For there is no spell against Jacob and no divination against Israel” (verse 23). The people rise like a lioness (verse 24).

Balak says, “Then neither curse them at all nor bless them at all!” (verse 25).
passages.hearers:
Balak's move to a new hill shows how he thinks. Perhaps the first place was unlucky. Perhaps the sight of so many tents was the trouble, so he chooses a spot where less of the camp can be seen. He treats the matter as one of angle and arrangement.

The second oracle answers that way of thinking directly. Balak has been dealing with God as he would deal with a human king, who can be pressed, paid or caught in a better mood until he goes back on his word. Verse 19 says that God is not like that. He does not lie. He does not give way under pressure. What he has promised, he does.

This is one of the great statements about God in the Old Testament. The hard question below looks at how it fits with other passages.

Verse 21 needs care. ‘He considers no disaster for Jacob’ does not mean that Israel had not sinned. The book has just spent ten chapters on Israel's sins, and God judged them. It means that God has no plan of ruin for his people that a hired curse could set off. Their failures are a matter between them and their God. They give their enemies no hold.

‘The shout of the King is among them’ pictures the cheer that goes up for a king among his soldiers. Israel has no human king. The king in the camp is the LORD, whose tent stands in the middle.

The pictures come from the world of herders and hunters. The wild ox was among the strongest animals people knew. The lioness and the lion stand for a strength that cannot be turned aside.

Verse 23 states the lesson of the three chapters: no spell, no divination. Everything Balak has paid for is worth nothing against a people God has chosen to bless.

Balak's replies become more desperate each time. First he complained. Then he tried another place. Now he begs Balaam to say nothing at all.
passages.later:
Samuel said the same to King Saul: “Moreover, the Glory of Israel does not lie or change His mind, for He is not a man, that He should change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29).

Paul rests the church's confidence on this: ‘For all the promises of God are “Yes” in Christ’ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

The letter to the Hebrews speaks of the comfort of God's unchanging purpose, that ‘it is impossible for God to lie’ (Hebrews 6:18).
passages.hard:
If God does not change his mind (verse 19), why do other passages say that he relented?

The same Hebrew verb, nacham, is used both ways. Here God is ‘not a man’ that he should change his mind. Yet after the golden calf, “the LORD relented from the calamity He had threatened to bring on His people” (Exodus 32:14). At Nineveh God ‘relented from the disaster’ he had announced (Jonah 3:10). And in this very book Moses prayed, and God pardoned (14:20).

Christians have explained this in more than one way. The classical view holds that God's nature and purpose never change. When the Bible says he relented, it describes how his dealings with people change as they change, told from the human side.

Others stress that God's warnings are often conditional on purpose. Jeremiah says so: if a nation God has warned turns from its evil, ‘then I will relent of the disaster I had planned to bring’ (Jeremiah 18:8). On this view, to relent when people repent is part of God's settled character, and not a change in it.

Some recent theologians go further and say that God truly adapts in his relationship with his creatures. Others strongly resist this.

These notes take no side. The setting of this verse gives the key to what it means here. Balak wanted a God who could be talked or bought out of a promise. Verse 19 says no. God does not break his word under pressure. That is fully in keeping with a God who shows mercy when people turn to him, which is what the other passages describe.
passages.asks: Balak hoped that a different view of things would produce a different word from God. Ask where you keep changing your angle on a matter, hoping God will say something other than what he has said. And ask which promise of God you most need to hear as fixed, one that he will not go back on.

passages.happening:
Balak does not give up. “Please come,” he says, ‘I will take you to another place. Perhaps it will please God that you curse them for me from there’ (verse 27).

He takes Balaam to the top of Peor, which looks out over the wasteland (verse 28). Balaam again asks for seven altars, seven bulls and seven rams, and Balak provides them (verses 29-30).
passages.hearers:
These four verses repeat the pattern a third time, and the repetition is part of the telling. Balak builds altars, Balaam goes aside, God gives a word, Balak objects, and Balak tries again. It has the rhythm of a comedy. The king is sure that with one more hill and seven more bulls the answer will change. By now forty-two animals have been offered across three sites.

His words show that he has heard nothing. ‘Perhaps it will please God.’ He has just been told that God is not a man who changes his mind.

The three heights, Bamoth-baal, Pisgah and Peor, lie along the edge of the high plain above the Jordan valley. Their exact places are uncertain. Two of them will matter again. From the range of Pisgah Moses will look across at the land before he dies (Deuteronomy 34:1). And at Peor, in chapter 25, Israel will do to itself what no curse from this hilltop could do.

A reader who knows that is meant to feel the weight of the name. Balak stands on Peor and cannot harm Israel. Soon Israel will come to Peor of its own accord.
passages.later:
Deuteronomy tells of Moses' last climb: “Then Moses went up from the plains of Moab to Mount Nebo, to the top of Pisgah, which faces Jericho” (Deuteronomy 34:1).

Hosea remembered Peor as the place where Israel's early promise was spoiled: ‘But they went to Baal-peor, and consecrated themselves to Shame’ (Hosea 9:10).
passages.asks: Balak could not hurt Israel from Peor, and Israel would soon harm itself there. Ask whether the greater danger to your faith comes from those who oppose you or from your own choices. And ask what you keep trying a third and a fourth time because you will not accept the answer you have been given.
